abstract: Full conformal prediction ordinarily relies on exchangeable data and symmetric fitting. We extend it with fixed calibration weights in [0,1], fixed algorithm tags, and a data-independent weighted random swap. Weights emphasize observations expected to resemble the test distribution; tags enable order-sensitive fitting. The swap connects miscoverage to high-residual indices, whose total normalized weight is at most alpha for any residual vector. Comparing original and swapped residual-vector distributions then gives finite-sample coverage at least 1 - alpha minus their weighted total-variation discrepancy. Under exchangeability this penalty vanishes, restoring nominal validity even with nonsymmetric fitting; otherwise, a small penalty limits undercoverage. When residuals are distinct, small discrepancy and normalized test weight also limit overcoverage. Related bounds cover split conformal and jackknife+, the latter with baseline 1 - 2 alpha. In simulations and electricity data, calibration weighting improves coverage, whereas weighted least-squares fitting can narrow intervals. On ordered electricity data, calibration weighting raises coverage from 85.2% to 89.0% but widens intervals; adding weighted fitting yields 89.3% coverage and narrower intervals. Both remain below the 90% target, and the width advantage disappears under random permutation. Election-data improvements also remain below target.
methods: Unlike symmetric fitting, nonsymmetric fitting need not produce exchangeable residuals. Prespecify calibration weights w_i in [0,1] and fixed tags; normalize by D = 1 + sum_i w_i, giving the test point weight 1/D. Draw K independently using these weights and swap observation K with the candidate test observation, keeping tags at their positions. At the true response, miscoverage implies that the test residual, now at index K, exceeds the swapped vector's weighted (1 - alpha)-quantile. The implication follows by replacing the test residual by infinity in the quantile and noting that each calibration weight is at most the test weight. For every residual vector, these high-residual indices carry normalized mass at most alpha. Independence allows averaging over K; comparing each swapped-vector event with its original-vector counterpart adds at most their total-variation distance. Hence miscoverage is bounded by alpha plus the weighted residual-distribution discrepancy, without algorithm symmetry or stability.
results: Table 2 separates improved coverage from narrower intervals in electricity-transfer prediction. In the original time order, unweighted full conformal with least squares yields 85.2% coverage and mean width 0.565. Keeping least squares but weighting calibration residuals raises coverage to 89.0% while increasing width to 0.606; adding weighted least-squares fitting gives 89.3% and width 0.527. Thus calibration weighting moves coverage toward the 90% target at a width cost, whereas weighted fitting produces narrower intervals with similar coverage in this setting. Neither weighted method reaches the target. In the randomly permuted, exchangeable control, these three methods have coverage 89.9%, 90.8%, and 90.8%, with widths 0.639, 0.652, and 0.663, respectively. The weighted-fitting width advantage does not persist after random permutation. These time-averaged comparisons neither establish coverage at every time point nor guarantee 90% coverage under arbitrary drift. For the randomized construction, a near-nominal coverage lower bound requires a small weighted swapped-residual total-variation term.
notes: Read-back: the abstract links the swap to controlled weighted ranks (Theorem 2b); Methods explains the quantile comparison and total-variation transfer (Section 7.2); Results separates calibration and fitting through Table 2's ordered and permuted comparisons. Coverage is marginal over data and the random swap. Retain Theorem 3's distinct-residual, small-discrepancy and small-test-weight conditions; jackknife+ starts at 1 - 2 alpha. Table 2 lacks uncertainty estimates and explicit width units; request clarification, without inventing either. Experiments cite equation (14) for nonsymmetric fitting, whereas Theorem 2b covers equation (20); confirm whether the randomized swap was implemented before attributing its guarantee to those results.
